en: Now begins the fourth chapter;
the tenth section of the second book.
I worship the most excellent gurus who composed the secondary texts of the Śrī Kalpasūtra.
[He honored] those named Śrīgārgya, Maśaka, Drāhyāyaṇa, and Kātyāyana.

In this *Kṣudrakalpasūtra*, having explained the deliberations on the *jyotiṣṭoma*—which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all sacrifices—by means of the first triad beginning with the first day (*pratipad*), the venerable teacher Gārgya Māṣaka, desiring hereafter to state the deliberations on the *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day rite)—which serves as the archetype for the multi-day sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*)—begins to set forth, in accordance with the Brāhmaṇas of other recensions, the deliberations concerning the twenty-two-fold variations of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* included within the *dvādaśāha*:
"Now, therefore, follow the deliberations regarding the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*" (1).

Now, immediately after the investigation into the *jyotis* which constitutes the fundamental nature [of the sacrifice], and because the investigation into the *jyotis* has thus been completed, the investigations concerning the *ṣaḍaha* (six-day rite) are commenced—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Within the *pṛṣṭhas* themselves, there is an investigation into various conceptualizations based on the differences among the *sāmans*. As it is stated in the *Nidāna*: "Now, the secondary procedure (*anukalpa*) for the *pṛṣṭhas*" refers to what is declared in the *Brāhmaṇa*; their status as a secondary procedure is due to their being undertaken immediately after the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, but not in the sense of being a substitute (*pratinidhi*), as is the case with *vrīhi* and *nīvāra* grains.

Since the term *vicāra* itself denotes various alternatives (*vividhakalpa*), these six-fold *vicāras* are optional alternatives (*vikalpante*) alongside the archetypal (*prākṛta*) six-day rite, like rice and barley. There are twenty-two of them: the first is the *pṛṣṭhya-stoma*; the second is the *nānā-pṛṣṭhya*; the third is the archetypal *parokṣa-pṛṣṭhya*; the fourth is the *sarva-parokṣa-pṛṣṭhya*; the fifth is the *ubhaya-parokṣa-pṛṣṭhya*; the sixth is the *upāṅkya-pṛṣṭhya*; and the seventh is the *anvāhārya-pṛṣṭhya*.

The twelfth day consists of the *upāṃśu-pṛṣṭhya* and *anvāhāryapṛṣṭhya*, with the eighth and ninth [days] following; the tenth is the *purastāj-jyotiḥ-ṣaḍaha*; the eleventh is the *upariṣṭāj-jyotiḥ-ṣaḍaha*; the twelfth day is the *bṛhadrathantara-purastāj-jyotiḥ-ṣaḍaha*; the thirteenth is the *bṛhadrathantara-upariṣṭāj-jyotiḥ-ṣaḍaha*; the fourteenth is the *parokṣāpārkyapṛṣṭhya*; the fifteenth is the *pratyakṣāpārkyapṛṣṭhya*; and the sixteenth is the *parokṣaprākyapṛṣṭhya*.

The seventeen-day sacrifice has the Prāyaṇīya and Pṛṣṭhya days performed in direct succession (*pratyakṣa*). The eighteen-day sacrifice has the Bṛhat and Rathantara as the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, with the *pṛṣṭhya* days performed in immediate succession (*anugṛhīta-pṛṣṭhya*). The nineteen-day sacrifice has the Bṛhat and Rathantara as the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, with the *pṛṣṭhya* days performed in indirect succession (*parokṣa-pṛṣṭhya*). The twenty-day sacrifice has various *pṛṣṭha* stotras, with the Bṛhat and Rathantara performed in immediate succession (*anugṛhīta-bṛhadrathantara*). The twenty-one-day sacrifice has various *pṛṣṭha* stotras, with the Bṛhat and Rathantara performed in more indirect succession (*anugṛhīta-bṛhadrathantara-parokṣatara*). The twenty-two-day sacrifice has the Brahmasāman as the *pṛṣṭha* stotra. ||1||
[The Pṛṣṭhya-stoma]:
Regarding that, he states its first essential nature:

"The six-day period (ṣaḍaha) with the Bṛhat and Rathantara as the pṛṣṭhas is arranged in a compact form (samūḍha). ||2|| This means that it is so called because in all six days of this six-day period, the Rathantara and Bṛhat are used as the pṛṣṭhas alternately. Since the Brāhmaṇa describes only the expanded form (vyūḍha), one might assume this [six-day period] is also expanded by virtue of being a modification of that; therefore, he says "arranged in a compact form" (samūḍha). ||2||
He states the ritual arrangement as being like that of the *pṛṣṭhya-stoma* seven-night sacrifice:
"Its ritual procedure is like that of the *pṛṣṭhya-stoma*, provided it is performed as a *yāhīnika*."
Thus [ends the discussion]. This has been explained. ||3||

Since the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) possesses the nature of both an *ahīna* and a *sattra*, and since the six-day period of *pṛṣṭha*-stotras (*pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*) is a constituent part thereof, the author states a specific rule regarding it when it occurs in various contexts—Chapter Four: Alternative Procedures for the *Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.
Now, if it belongs to the *sattra*, being that very same [period], it has the *gaurīvita* as its *svara*. 4.

Thus [it is stated]. This is clear. Here, on the fourth day, according to the opinion of the author of the *Kalpa*, the Gaurīvita should be performed as the *ṣoḍaśisāman* for the *nānadastotrīya*. Alternatively, the Gaurīvita is the *ṣoḍaśisāman* among the *svarāj* verses beginning with "indraṃ juṣasva. This is stated in the *Nidāna*: "Now, regarding the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* *pṛṣṭhas* in the twelve-day sacrifice," and so on, up to the end of the section: "They do not think so; rather, here only the *svarāj* verses are to be understood. For these are the original (*prākṛta*) ones."

These are also more logical, and they apply everywhere in all sacrifices where there is no specific instruction; by this, the *ṣoḍaśi-stotra* of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) characterized by the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* *pṛṣṭha*-stotras has been explained—both that which occurs in the variations of the six-day period and that which occurs in the *saṃsad*s. Thus it is stated twice: "and that which occurs in the *saṃsad*s. This is clear. 4.
[The *nānāpṛṣṭhya*]:
He states the nature of the second [type]:
"Now, therefore, follows the *nānāpṛṣṭhya* six-day rite. (5)

Thus: "Various" means various *pṛṣṭhas*. A collection of these is "various *pṛṣṭhas*" (*nānāpṛṣṭhya*). The suffix *yañ* is applied according to the rule "addition for [words ending in] *pṛṣṭha*. The *pṛṣṭhas* are the Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata. ||5||
Whether gathered together or spread out. ||6||
Thus, according to the opinion of another Vedic school. ||6||

And according to our own Brāhmaṇa tradition, having raised the objection that there is no fixed rule regarding the *samūḍha* and *vyūḍha* arrangements, he states the rule: "But it is indeed the *samūḍha* [that is used]. (7)

Thus [it is said]. The word *tu* (but) serves to exclude other alternatives. The particle *eva* (only/just) is for the purpose of restriction. Because this *ṣaḍaha* (six-day rite) is accomplished by means of six days, because it is interrupted by the non-completion of the nine-night (*navarātra*) period, and because there is an absence of the *vyūḍha* (interlaced) arrangement for the *triṣṭubh* metre, the *samūḍha* (uninterlaced) alone is superior. Where the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* possesses the same metres (*sachandoma*), there is an option between the *vyūḍha* and the *samūḍha*; but where it lacks the same metres (*vicchandoma*), there is only the *samūḍha*—this is the intention of the Teacher.
This is stated in the *Nidānasūtra*: "In that case also, O Brāhmaṇa, it is as follows: 'The *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] cannot be expanded without the *chandomas*. (7)
He states the arrangement: "Its ritual procedure is like that of the seasons, provided it is a six-day rite for those who perform the *āhīna* sacrifices. (8)
Thus it is; this is clear. ||8||
Now, if that very same [chant] is accompanied by the *sāman*, it possesses the *gaurīvita* tone. ||9||
Thus [ends the discussion]. This has been explained. ||9||
[The Parokṣapṛṣṭhya] He states the nature of the third [six-day period]:
"Now, therefore, follows the six-day period with the parokṣa pṛṣṭhas. (10)
Thus; he for whom the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are the Pṛṣṭha-stotras when [the sacrifice] is out of sight is described in that manner. ||10||
He states the ritual arrangement:
"Its ritual procedure is as follows: for the first day, the *kaṇvarathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant, with the verse 'abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ. For the second day—'tvāmiddhi havāmahe'.
[End of] Chapter Four: The Ritual Arrangements for the *Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

Thus [ends] the *Bṛhannidhana* [chant] for the *Vārka-jambha*, or the *Kaṇva-bṛhat*. The second [day] belongs to these [verses] beginning with "ā tvā sahasram ā śatam. The subsequent four-day period has its *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] well-known. 11.

Thus: the statement "ā tvā sahasram" is for the purpose of demonstrating its origin from the *kaṇva-bṛhat*, but it is not for the purpose of being a *stotrīya* verse here. It is called "one whose back [chapters] are well-known" (*prajñātapṛṣṭha*) because in that third to fourth four-day period (*caturahe*), the *vairūpa*, *vairāja*, *śākvara*, and *vāravantīya* chants are well-known and directly perceived; thus it is so designated. ||11||
Regarding the nature of the fourth [rite], he says: "Now, therefore, follows the six-day rite consisting entirely of indirect (parokṣa) responses. (12)
Thus: he is so described because all his *pṛṣṭha* stotras—the Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata—are performed indirectly (*parokṣa*). ||12||

Regarding the commonality of the indirect (*parokṣa*) *sāmans* for the six *pṛṣṭhas*, its ritual procedure is as follows: these very same [sāmans] are used for the *pṛṣṭhas* of the first and second days. 13.
Thus: [the sacrifice is performed] with the Kaṇvarathantara and the Kaṇvabṛhatī, or with the Kaṇvarathantara and the Bṛhannidhana Vārkajambha. ||13||
For the third day: "O Indra, if a hundred [are yours]"—with this, the *upāśu* chant is either the short *bṛhat* or the *antarikṣa*. 14.
Thus [it is said]. This is clear. ||14||
In the world of the intermediate space, one should fashion the *vairūpa* chant according to the *añjas*. ||15||
Thus, during the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, one should sing the Añjovairūpa at the place of the intermediate region (antarikṣa) upon the triplet beginning with "abhi somāsaḥ. This is the meaning. ||15||
In the place of the *pṛṣṭha*, he states another *sāman* as an alternative:
"Or the *mahāvaiṣṭambha*. (16)

Thus [it is said]. "Yad dyāvaḥ" is indeed a triplet (ṛca). To avoid the fault of wandering about, he prescribes another Sāman on the back of the Brahman priest: "The Kāṇva [Sāman] with an Abhinidhana in the world of Mahāvaiṣṭambha.
Thus [it is said]. "Vayaṃ gha tvā" is indeed a triplet.
For the fourth day: "Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate thee"—this is the Ṛṣabha-vairāja, belonging to Sahoda or Dīrghatamas, ending with "hāu piba. ||18||
Thus; the meaning is that the second [stotra] is to be sung in the *yoni* and in the two *sahodairghatamas* verses. ||18||
He states another alternative: "The Vairāja of Vasiṣṭha, or the one beginning with 'agniṃ naro'—the latter of these two. (19)
Thus it is clear. ||16||
On the fifth day, the verses beginning with "trikaḍrukeṣu mahiṣo yavāśiram" are those that always possess their own calves.

Thus it is clear. Because these [verses] contain the nidhana of the two perceptible words *pracetana* and *pracetaya* situated in the *śakvarī* meters, they are not entirely cryptic; thus [the rule applies] to those that have permanent calves. ||20||
The Fourth Chapter: Alternative Forms of the Pṛṣṭhya-Ṣaḍaha.
Regarding the variation of the Sāmans, it says: "Or, first among the Atiṣaṅgas—on these Gāyatrīs and Anuṣṭubhs beginning with *indrāyāhi citrabhāno*, *yadindra citram*, and *iha na*" (21).

Thus it is said. This has been explained. Because of the combination of the *gāyatrī* and *anuṣṭubh* meters, they consist of seven feet; thus, by virtue of being *śakvarī*s, their connection with the *simā*s is well-established. Since there is no other *sāman* in these manifest (*pratyakṣa*) verses beginning with "vidā maghavan," the Teacher has prescribed another *sāman* for other verses. As it is stated in the *Nidāna*: "But not in the fifth [book], because of the difference; for there is no other [sāman] among the *mahānāmnī*s. And in the *Sūtra*: "For no other *sāman* occurs in these [verses]; even when performing the *parokṣa* [sāmans] during the *pṛṣṭha-stotras*, one does not perform the *nityavat-sā*s on these [verses]. (21)
The Vāravantīya is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra of the sixth day.
Thus [ends the discussion]. This has been explained. ||22||

If it is objected: "In the original *ṣaḍaha* sacrifice, since the *vāravantīya* itself is directly perceived as the *pṛṣṭha* chant, how can there be an injunction here for a *pṛṣṭha* chant that is not directly perceived?"—it is not so. For in all cases, it is the *revatī* verses alone that are directly perceived. Even in the *Taittirīya* and other recensions, when the six *pṛṣṭhas* are mentioned, only the *revatīs* are mentioned; thus, in the triplet beginning with "revatīr naḥ," the *vāravantīya* is indeed indirect (*pārokṣya*). Precisely for this reason, since the *revatīs* are directly perceived in the *mādhyandina-pavamāna*, he prescribes another *sāman* that is indirect in its place: "In the world of the *revatīs*, [there is] the *dārḍhacyuta*. (23)

Thus it is said. This has been explained. Because the *dārḍhacyuta* serves as the *nidhana*, there is an absence of the fault of repetition (*jāmi*), just as in the archetypal form (*prakṛti*). ||23||
In order to conform to the Vedic injunction, "They begin with the Bṛhatī by means of the Aiḍa [verse]," he states the exchange of the two nostrils of the bull:
"He exchanges the two nostrils of the bull. (24)
Thus [ends the section]. ||24||
Thus ends the tenth section in the second chapter. || 0 ||
The eleventh section [dealing with the *pṛṣṭhya* period when both are indirect] states the nature of the fifth day:
Now, therefore, follows the six-day period characterized by *pṛṣṭha* chants that are indirect on both sides.
Thus [ends the first verse].
He himself explains the word "both": "from the Rigveda and from the Samaveda. (2)
Thus [ends the second section].
He states the arrangement:
"Its ritual procedure is as follows: for the first day, the *kaṇvarathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant, [with the verse] 'abhitvā pūrvapītaye'. (3)
On the second day: "tvaṃ hyehi cerava" with the *bṛhat* as the *nidhana*, or the *vārkajambha*; or the *kaṇvabṛhat*.
Chapter Four: The alternative forms of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.
Of these [verses], "ā tvā sahasramāśatam" is the second.
On the third day, for the verse "O Indra, as many as you are," the *upaśa* chant is the short *bṛhat*; it is indeed the intermediate space.
In the world of the intermediate space, one should fashion the Añjovairūpa brick, or the Mahāvaiṣṭambha.
In the world [of the Sāman], the *abhinidhana* of the *mahāvaiṣṭambha* belongs to Kāṇva.
For the fourth day: "Hear the call of the pressing-stone as it drinks," [is] the Ṛṣabha-vairāja; or [it is] the Sahoda of Dīrghatamas; and "Hāu! Drink!"—this [is the concluding syllable]. ||8||

[The *dhur*] following the two [verses] "Of Vasiṣṭha" and "O men, the Vairāja for Agni" belongs to the fifth day. [The *dhur*] "Forward for him the chariot" (*proṣvasmai puroratham*) is like the constant ones. Or rather, the first of the *atīṣaṅga* verses—namely, "Come to Indra, O bright-rayed one" (*indrāyāhi citrabhāno*), "When, O Indra, the wonderful [thing] here" (*yadindra citrama iha*), and "No" (*nā*)—are in *gāyatrī* and *anuṣṭubh* meters.
On the sixth day, for these very [deities], the Vāravantīya is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra with the verse beginning "O wealthy one, praise this."
In the world of the Revatīs, it causes the firmness to fall; it exchanges [it] for the nostril of the bull.

Thus; it is to be explained as before. Since the triplet beginning with *pro ṣvasmai* consists of seven verses by its very nature, the indirect application (*pārokṣya*) of the *śakvarī* meter is entirely appropriate. ||14||
Thus ends the eleventh section of the second chapter. ||15||
Twelfth Section: [The Upāṃśu-pṛṣṭhya and Anvāhārya-pṛṣṭhya].
He states the nature of the sixth and seventh [days]:
Now, therefore, follow the two six-day periods characterized by the Upāṃśu-pṛṣṭha and the Anvāhārya-pṛṣṭha.

Thus: the word *aṅka* denotes a place. Because they deserve a place (*aṅka*) near (*upa*) the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] during the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, they are called *upāṅkyāni*. That [sacrifice] in which those *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are present is thus described. Following (*anu*) the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ, in the Ārbhava [pavamāna], those *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] which are to be arranged (*āhāryāṇi*) or prepared (*kalpyāni*) are present; that [sacrifice] is thus described. (1) He states the arrangement:

The ritual procedure for these two is as follows: the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are performed with directly audible verses (*pratyakṣa*) during the directly audible *pṛṣṭha-stotrīyas*; they are performed with verses not directly audible (*parokṣa*) during the midday [pressings]. For five of the days, they are in *bṛhatī* meters; for the sixth day, they are in *gāyatrī* meters. This is the six-day period characterized by the *upāṅkya-pṛṣṭha*.

Thus [it is said]. This is clear. The arrangement of this is as follows. Herein is the underlying cause (nidāna): Now follows the alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) for the *pṛṣṭha* days. On the first day, in place of the *rathantara-parokṣa*, the two [sāmans] consisting of three *nidhanas* and one with the *nidhana* in the middle should be placed within the *tṛca*. Regarding the chanting of the verses for the sake of stability, this is the fourth chapter: The Alternative Procedures for the *Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

"Therefore, they do not perform the *apaciti* (reverential treatment) of the *brahmarahasya* on the *bṛhadrathantara-ekarccas*. Regarding the first day: the *sāmatṛcas* for the *gāyatra-aśva-soma-sāmans* are "pra somāso vipaścitaḥ" (in three verses). The *kaṇvarathantara* is [performed] on three verses beginning with "pra soma devavītaye. The *auśana* is the last, "pra tu drava," [also] on three verses. Alternatively, here the *Nidānasūtra* states: "The *ekarccas* are either together with the obligatory ones, or the *yajñagauṅgava* is in the middle, while the *sāmatṛcas* are in the *bṛhatī*."

"Forward, O wise Soma-stalks"—these are the *gāyatrāśvasoma* *sāmans*, consisting of triplets (*tṛcas*). "Forward, O divine Soma"—these are the *kaṇvarathantara*, *pajra*, and *audhājaya* *sāmans*, consisting of triplets; or alternatively, the *kaṇvarathantara*, *gauṅgava*, and *audhājaya*. The *auśana* is the final one, performed on three verses. The rest is the same as the first [day]. Thus it is for the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) when it functions as a sacrificial session (*sattra*), and for the *gavāmayana*.

In the *Anukalpa* of the *Abhīvarta-kāleya*, however, the introductory rule (*nidāna*) here is as follows: on the first day, there are the three-verse *sāmans* consisting of the *Rathantara*, *Abhīvarta*, and *Yaudhājaya*. By implication, this is like the *Jami-vrata* and *Garbhivat*. At the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*), in the *Bṛhatī* [meter], the specific rule is that there are the three-verse *sāmans* consisting of the *Kaṇva-rathantara*, *Abhīvarta*, and *Yaudhājaya*. Alternatively, the introductory rule here is: "All are indeed single-verse [stotras]. And nine [verses] in the *Bṛhatī*, having been separated by the *Pajra* and *Gauṅgava*, [are placed] three times in the very first [turn].

The verses beginning with "pra soma devavītaye" are for the Kaṇvarathantara and Pajra [stotras] on the first day; the Sāman-trikas are the Abhīvarta, Gauṅgava, and Auddhājava; and the Auśana is the last one, performed on a single verse. This is the distinction. Here, even in the Mādhyandina Pavamāna, the duties (dharmas) of the Pṛṣṭha [stotra] must be performed. Regarding this, it is stated in the Nidāna: "They should be performed, say the Teachers, because through their application these duties belong to them; moreover, we see that they are performed even when they have departed from their original place."

Regarding the second day: here is the underlying rule (*nidāna*). For the daily [stotras], there are the *Dairghaśravasa*, *Aidhātitha*, *Pūrvābhiśava*, *Hārāyaṇa*, and *Kaulmalabarhiṣa* chants. At the midday pressing, on the *Bṛhatī* verses, the triple-verse *sāman*s are the *Aiḍamāyāsya*, *Atriṇidhana*, *Āyāsya*, and *Dairghaśravasa*. On the three [verses] of the *Kaṇvabṛhat*, there is either the *Bṛhannidhana* or the *Vārkajambha*. The rest is the same as on the second day.

Regarding the *abhīvarta*, *kāleya*, and *anukalpa* chants, the introductory context (*nidāna*) here concerns the second day. "Beginning with that" means beginning with the *āgantu* and so forth; "consisting of the *bṛhat* and so forth" means the *sāman*-verses (*sāmatṛc*) beginning with the *bṛhat*. Regarding the phrase "beginning with the *bārhatādyāt*": a *sāman* produced from a *bṛhatī* verse is called *bārhatam*; "beginning with the *bārhatādyāt*" means the *aiḍa*, *āyāsya*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya* *sāman*-verses. "As I know" [refers to this]. The meaning of this is as follows: on the second day, beginning with that [the *āgantu*], there are the *sāman*-verses beginning with the *bṛhat*. "Beginning with the *bārhatādyāt*" means the *sāman*-verses such as the *aiḍa*, *āyāsya*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya*, which are produced from the *bṛhatī* meter. "As I know" [refers to this].

In the *gavāmayana* sacrifice, during the original six-day period (*prakṛta-ṣaḍaha*), I understand that the *aiḍa*, *māyāsya*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya* *sāman*-verses are arranged exactly as prescribed by the author of the ritual manual (*kalpakāra*). However, in the *bṛhatī* [stoma], the *aiḍa*, *māyāsya*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya* *sāman*-verses consist of three verses each; or alternatively, the *kaṇva-bṛhat*, *dairghaśravasa*, *triṇidhana-māyāsya* *sāman*-verses consisting of three verses each; or else the *bṛhannidhana-vārka-jambha*, *dairghaśravasa*, *triṇidhana-māyāsya* [verses]. This is the distinction. Here, even in the *mādhyandina-pavamāna*, the duties pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] must be performed.

This is the third day. Regarding this, the *nidāna* states: "The *āgantuka* [verses] and the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] are at the end. For the first [turn], the *paurumadga* [sāman] beginning with "abhi soma" is used; the *sāmatṛcas* of Gautama, Añjovairūpa, and Aidhātitha; and the *antarikṣa* [sāman] in the three [verses]. The *āṣkāraṇidhana* [sāman] is for the *adhyāsyā*. Alternatively, in the *bṛhatī* meter, the *paurumadga* beginning with "abhi soma" is for the first [turn]; the *sāmatṛcas* of Gautama, Antarikṣa, and Aidhātitha; the short *bṛhat* [sāman] as the *upaśa* in the three [verses]; and the *āṣkāraṇidhana* [sāman] is for the *adhyāsyā*.
Or rather, if the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] here has the *nidhana* like the *nidāna*, then in the third [section], the fourth chapter is "The Alternatives for the *Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*."

"In the *bṛhatī* [stoma], the first is reversed. Regarding this: the *paurumadga* [sāman] "abhi soma" is [chanted] on the first [verse]; the *mahāvaiṣṭambha* on three [verses]; the *sāmatṛcas* consisting of the *maidhātitha*, *antarikṣa*, and *gautama* [sāmans]; the *āṣkāraṇidhana* on the *adhyāsya*; and the *kāṇva* [sāman] "vayaṃ gha tvā" with the *abhinidhana* for the *brahman*. The rest is the same as the third [day]. However, regarding the alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) for the *abhīvarta* and *kāleya*, the *nidāna* states here: "Then, the *pṛṣṭha* [laud] lacks a *nidhana*; the *gāyatra* is chanted on one [verse] during the third and fifth [days]."

"Regarding the second and third days": this is the meaning. On the third and fifth days, if the *pṛṣṭha* stotra is the *aiḍa* sāman without a *nidhana*, then for the two sāmans on the second and third [verses], the performance of a single verse (*ekarcakaraṇa*) must be carried out. "Uccā te" is the *gāyatra* on one verse; the *kṣullakavaiṣṭambha* on three verses. "Abhi soma" refers to the *paurumadga*, *gautama*, and *antarikṣa* as triple-verse sāmans (*sāmatṛcas*). In that same triple-verse sequence, the *abhīvarta*, *kāleya*, and *maidhātitha* are also triple-verse sāmans.

In the three [verses], there is the *hrasvā* and the *bṛhadupaśā*. In the *āṣkāra-nidhana* [sāman], it is the middle of the *asyā*. Or rather, in the place of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), there is the *añjovairūpa*; the distinction is that "the intermediate space" is in the place of the *hrasvā-bṛhadupaśā*. Or rather, in the two triplets of the *gāyatra-kṣullaka-vaiṣṭambha*, [there is] "uccā te"; in the first [verse], the *paurumadga* [is used]. The *mahāvaiṣṭambha* and *aidhātitha* are the triplet-sāmans for the intermediate spaces. In that very triplet, the *abhīvarta*, *kāleya*, and *gautama* are the triplet-sāmans.
The *āṣkāranidhana* is to be chanted upon the *madhyāsyā*. This is the distinction. Here, even in the *mādhyandina-pavamāna*, the rites pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are to be performed.

For the fourth day: on the *bṛhatī* [verse], the *sāman*-triplets are the *āṣṭādaṃṣṭra*, the *ābhīśava*, the *svaḥpṛṣṭha*, and the *āṅgirasa*. On three [verses] beginning with the *ābhīśava*, the *ṛṣabha-vairāja* is performed on three [verses], or the *sahodairghatamasa*, or the *vasiṣṭhasya vairāja*. The rest is the same as the fourth day. However, according to the alternative for the *abhīvarta-kāleya*, the *sāman*-triplets on the *bṛhatī* are the *āṣṭādaṃṣṭra*, the *abhīvarta*, and the *kāleya*. On that same triplet, the *sāman*-triplets are the *ābhīśava-uttara*, the *svaḥpṛṣṭha*, the *āṅgirasa*, and those beginning with the *ābhīśava*. The *ṛṣabha*...

The Vairāja [Sāman] is used for the three [verses]. Or it is the Vairāja of Vasiṣṭha, or that of Dīrghatamas with the word *saha*. This is the distinction. Here, even in the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, the ritual characteristics (*dharma*) of the Pṛṣṭha-stotra should be performed.

Regarding the fifth day: here the underlying principle (*nidāna*) is that the rule applies by transposing [the elements] on the fifth and the last days. On the *bṛhatī* [verse], the *sāman*-triplets are "Soma uṣva," the Mānava, the Ānūpa, and the *triṇidhana*; the Vāma, Hārāyaṇa, and Nityavatsa are on the triplets. Or else, the first of the *atīṣaṅga* [verses]. Or alternatively: the *sāman*-triplets are "Soma uṣva," the Mānava, the Ānūpa, and the Vāma; the *triṇidhana* and Hārāyaṇa are on two triplets; the Nityavatsa is on three verses. Or else, the first of the *atīṣaṅga* [verses].

The rest is the same as the fifth [chapter]. However, in the alternative arrangement for the *abhīvarta*, *kāleya*, and others: the *gāyatra* "arṣā soma" is used on a single verse; the *yaṇva*, *śākala*, and *vārśa* are used on triplets (*tṛca*); the *mānava* "some uṣva" is used on three verses; the *ānūpa* is used on the first verse; the *triṇidhana* of Agni is used on three verses; the *vāma*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya* are *sāman*-triplets; the *hārāyaṇa* is used on a single verse; and the *nityavat-sāmans* are used on three verses. Or else, the first of the *atīṣaṅga* hymns may be used; or alternatively, the *gāyatra* "arṣā soma" [is used].

In one [verse]: the *yaṇva*, *śākala*, and *vārṣa* [are used] in *tṛcas*. The *soma uṣva* of the Mānava [school] is used in three [verses]. The *ānūpa* is used in one [verse]. The *vāma*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya* are *sāman-tṛcas*.
The Fourth Chapter: Alternatives for the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

The *triṇidhana* of Agni is used in three [verses]. The *hārāyaṇa* is used in one [verse]. The *nityavat-sāman* is used in three [verses], or alternatively, the first of the *atīṣaṅga* [sāmans]. This is the distinction. Here, even in the *mādhyandina-pavamāna*, the duties pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* should be performed.

Regarding the sixth day: here the underlying principle (*nidāna*) is that because the sixth day is characterized by two *pṛṣṭha* chants, [the *sāmans*] should be placed both before and after; this applies likewise to the *upāṅkya*, *pṛṣṭha-anvāhārya*, and *pṛṣṭha* [chants]. For the triplet verses (*tṛca*), there are the *gāyatra*, *aiṣovṛdhīya*, *krauñca*, *vājadāvarya*, *raivata*, and *dārḍhacyuta* [sāmans] for Indra, O Indu. For the triplet verses, there are the *svāra*, *aukṣṇorandhra*, *aiḍa*, *aukṣṇorandhra*, and *varuṇasāman* [sāmans] for the triplet verses beginning with "mṛjyamānaḥ. And for the triplet verses, there are the *vājajit*, *kaulmalabarhiṣa*, and *goṣṭha* [sāmans].

The rest is the same as the sixth [stotra]. However, in the alternative form of the *abhīvarta* and *kāleya*, the *mṛjyamāna* [verse] is in the *bṛhatī* meter; the *svāra* and *aukṣṇorandhra* [melodies] are in three verses. The *aiḍa*, *aukṣṇorandhra*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya* constitute the *sāmatṛcas*. The *kaulmalabarhiṣa* is in three verses. The *vājajit*, *varuṇasāman*, and *goṣṭha* constitute the *sāmatṛcas*; this is the distinction. Here, even in the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, the duties pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] must be performed. 2.
He states the second [view]:

"Those same [verses] are used for the *anuṣṭubh* verses of the *ārbhava* [śastra] during the five days; for the sixth day, they are used for the *gāyatrī* verses. That is the *anvāhāryapṛṣṭha* six-day period. ||3||

Thus it is stated; this is clear. Herein is its arrangement. The underlying reason (*nidāna*) for this is as follows: Now, regarding the alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) for the *pṛṣṭha* chants. On the first day, in the case of the *rathantara* being unperceived (*parokṣa*), the two [chants] belonging to the *triṇidhana* and *adhyenidhana* should take the place of those situated in the *tṛca*. For it is said in the *Pratiṣṭhā*, the *Uha-gīti*, and the *Brahma-rahasya*: "Therefore, they do not perform the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* on a single verse (*ekarca*). The *aiḍa* and *kāva* [sāmans] are placed on a single verse at the end; or else the *vaikhānasa*. This is because of the precedent of favoring the *iḍā*, due to the impossibility of [fitting] the *stomas*, and because of the observation of the *udbhid* and *ekatrika* [chant structures].

In the Ārbhava [Śastra], the verses beginning with *pra somāso madacyutaḥ* are the Gāyatra-saṃhitā in the first [turn]. In the Sapha-akṣāra, the two single-verse hymns begin with *ayā pavasva* and *pavate haryataḥ*. The Gaurīvita is in one verse beginning with *pra sunvānaḥ*. The Kaṇvarathantara is in three verses. The Aiḍa and Kāva are in one verse beginning with *abhipriyāṇi*; or else the Vaikhānasa; or else, according to the Nidāna, the single-verse hymns are recited together with the obligatory ones. Or, within the obligatory Anuṣṭubhs, the Pṛṣṭha and Audala are in the first [turn]. All [the rest] are single-verse hymns.

In the *triṇidhana* [stotra], because of the practice of favoring the *nidhana*, the end of the *svara* [is reached] through the perspective of logic; thus there is the *gīti* of the *viśālārtha*. "pra somāso madacyutaḥ" is for the *gāyatra-saṃhitā*; "ayā pavasva pavate" is for the *sapha-akṣāra*; "pra sunvānaḥ" is for the *gaurīvitakaṇvarathantaraudalagautama* chants, all in the first [verse] alone. "abhi priyāṇi" is the final *svāra-kāva* in a single [verse]. The rest is the same as the first. Here, even in the *ārbhavapavamāna*, the duties of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are to be performed.

Regarding the second day: here is the underlying principle—that the *anurūpas* consist of *ānuṣṭubha* verses, and for the *agniṣṭomasāman* on the second and fifth days of the *āhīnika* [rite], they are performed in the *svāra* [melody].

When there is a connection with adventitious [verses], the *tṛcas* (triplets) are not to be used, because the *nityānugraha-stoma* (the permanent favoring-stoma) is applicable; rather, single verses (*ekarccas*) are to be employed. "That which is thy intoxication" (*yaste madaḥ*) is for the Gāyatra-hāviṣmat in the first [verse]. "Flow, O Pavamāna, toward Indra" (*pavasvendramaccha*) is for the Śaṅku-sujñāna in the two single verses. "This one, O Pūṣan" (*ayaṃ pūṣā*) is for the Gaurīvita-maiḍa-krauñca in the first [verse]. The *svāra-krauñca* is in three [verses]; the *kaṇva-bṛhat* is in three [verses]; or the *bṛhannidhana-vārkajaṃbha*. The rest is the same as the second [stotra]. Here, even in the Ārbhava-pavamāna, the duties of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are to be performed.

Regarding the third day: here the *nidāna* states that on the third day, at the *ārbhava* [laud], there is a *gāyatra* [sāman] on a single verse. By implication, the transition to the insertion (*āvāpa*) is like that of the *abhiṣecanīya*. Likewise for the two following days; thus ends the fourth chapter: "The Alternative Forms of the *Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*. At the *ārbhava*, in the section concerning the intermediate region (*antarikṣapakṣa*), there is the *gāyatra-kṣullaka-vaiṣṭambha* [sāman] on the verse beginning "uccā te" (at the midday pressing). The *paurumadga* [sāman] begins with "abhi soma" on the first verse. The *ubhayatastobha-gautama-añjovairūpa* [sāmans] are on the two triplets (*ṛcas*). The *āṣkāra-nidhana* [sāman] is on the middle verse.

In the Ārbhava [Śastra], on the Mahāvaiṣṭambha side, the Pṛṣṭhas consist of the Vairūpa, the Vāmadevya, the Abhinidhana, and the Kāṇva-raurava Sāmans. The Gāyatra is on one verse with the words *tisro vācaḥ*. The Pāṣṭhauha is on three verses. The Vācasāma and Śaukta are on two single verses (*ekarcca*) with the words *ā sosakhāyaḥ*. The Gaurīvit and Triṇidhana-Tvāṣṭrī Sāmans are on the first verse with the words *sutāso me*. The Antarikṣasvāra and Tvāṣṭrī Sāmans are on two triplets (*tṛca*). The Ariṣṭa is the last, beginning with *pavitraṃ te*.

Alternatively: *sutāso me* and the *Gaurīvita-triṇidhana* and *Tvāṣṭrī-sāmans* are on the first [verse]; the *hrasva*, the *bṛhat-upaśā*, and the *svāra-tvāṣṭrī-sāmans* are on the two triplets; *pavitraṃ te* is the final *ariṣṭa*. Alternatively, the *Nidāna* states: "In the third [day], the last [verse] is an *anuṣṭubh*, and the [sāman] is adventitious (*āgantuka*). Thus, *sutāso me* and the *Gaurīvita-triṇidhana* and *Tvāṣṭrī-sāmans* are on the first; the *svāra-tvāṣṭrī-sāman* and the *mahāvaiṣṭambha* are on the two triplets. The rest is the same as the third day.
Here, even in the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, the duties of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] are to be performed.

Regarding the fourth day: here the *nidāna* is that there is a *gāyatra* hymn on a single verse in the *ārbhava* [śastra]. By implication, the transition (*āvāpa*) follows the *anuṣṭubh* verses, as in the *abhiṣecanīya*. Likewise, if there is a repetition (*jāmi*) in the two following [days], it occurs at the end of the two fixed [verses]. In the middle, when they are reversed, there is a transposition (*vyatyāsa*) consisting of a single verse and a triplet. Such is the meaning of "likewise in the two following. This refers to the fourth and fifth days. "The seer of heaven, dear" (*pari priyā divaḥ kaviḥ*) is the *gāyatra* on a single verse; the *aurṇāyava* is on three verses.

For "tvaṃ hyaṅga daivyasomaḥ" and "pūtāna ūrmiṇā," there are two triplets (ṛcas) from the Bṛhat-kātīṣādīya collection. For "purojitī," there is one verse from the Nānada collection. For "ṛṣabha-vairāja," there are three verses. Or [one may use] the "sahoda" of Dīrghatamas, or the "vairāja" of Vasiṣṭha. For "śyāvāśva," there is one verse; for "āndhīgava," there are three verses. Alternatively, regarding this, the *Nidāna* states: "In the fourth [section], the three beginning with the *kakubh* are single-verse [stotras]; the others occupy the place of triplets. For "pari priyā divaḥ kaviḥ," there are two triplets from the Gāyatra-Urṇāyava collection.

For "tvaṃ hyaṅga daivyasomaḥ punāna ūrmiṇā" [is used] in the two single-verse [stotras] of the Bṛhat-kātīṣādīya; "purojitī" [is used] in the Nānada for one verse; the Vṛṣabha-vairāja [is used] in three verses, or the Sahoda of Dīrghatamas, or the Vairāja of Vasiṣṭha; the Śyāvāśva and Āndhīgava [are used] in two triplets; the rest is the same as with the fourth [stotra]. But in the Samūḍha, the Uṣṇih and Kakubh [are used] in two single verses; "purojitī" [is used] in the Nānada for one verse; the Āndhīgava and Śyāvāśva [are used] in two triplets; and the Vṛṣabha-vairāja [is used] in three verses.

Either the *sahoda* with *dīrghatamas*, or Vasiṣṭha’s *vairāja*; the *lauśa* beginning with "pra ta āśvinīḥ" is the final [stotra]—this is the distinction. Here, even in the Ārbhavapavamāna, the duties (*dharmas*) pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are to be performed.

For the fifth day: at the Ārbhava Pavamāna, "asāvyaṃśurmadāya" is the Gāyatra [Sāman] on a single verse; the Santani on three verses; and "abhi dyumnam," "prāṇā," and "śiśuḥ" are the Cyāvana and Krośa on two single verses. "pavasva vājasātaye" is the Gorīvita, Ṛṣabha, Śākvara, Pārtha, Aṣṭeḍa, Pada, Stobha, and Ātreya on triple verses; these are the Nityavat-sāmans on three verses, or else the first of the Atīṣaṅgas. Regarding the Samūḍha, the Nidāna states: "In the Samūḍha, the Śuddhāśuddhīya is like the Prāvṛṣābhinidhana."

"Pavasva vājasātaye" [is the first verse]; then the Gaurīvita, Nityavatsa, Śuddhāśuddhīya, Ṛṣabha, Śākvara, Ākūpāra, Aṣṭeḍa, Padastobha—these are to be used in the triads (tṛcas). Alternatively, the first of the Atīṣaṅgas may take the place of the Nityavatsas. The rest is the same as with the fifth [laud]. Here, in the Ārbhava-pavamāna as well, the dharmas of the Pṛṣṭhas are to be performed.
The Fourth Chapter: Substitutes for the Pṛṣṭhya-Ṣaḍaha;

Now, regarding the sixth day. Herein is the underlying principle (*nidāna*): because on the sixth day there is a sense of dual ownership over the *pṛṣṭha* chants, it should occur both before and after [the central portion]—thus it is for both the *upāṅkya-pṛṣṭha* and the *anvāhārya-pṛṣṭha* as well—and the additional *pṛṣṭha* chant is at the end.

*parisvāno giriṣṭhāḥ*—these are the *gāyatravaidanvata*, *ādyavaidanvata*, *caturthavaidanvata*, and *dārḍhacyuta* [sāmans]. *sa sutaṃ vaḥ sakha*—these two triplets are for Dīrghakārṇaśravas. *somāḥ pavanta indavaḥ*—these triplets of *sāman*s are the *gaurīvitam*, *madhuścunnidhana*, and *ākūpāra*. *vāṅnidhana*, *krauñcaiḍa*, and *krauñca* are for the two triplets. Or alternatively: for Dīrghakārṇaśravas, they are for single verses; the *gaurīvitam* is for one verse.

The *madhuścut* is the *nidhana*, the *vāṅnidhana* is the *nidhana*, and the *krauñca*, *ākūpara*, and *aiḍa* are the *krauñca*s in the triple-verses (*tṛca*s). The rest is the same as the sixth [laud]. Here, in the Ārbhava-pavamāna as well, the duties of the *pṛṣṭha* [laud] are to be performed.
Regarding the *upāṅkyapṛṣṭha* and *anvāhāryapṛṣṭhya* [six-day periods], he states the nature of the eighth and ninth [days] according to their different varieties:
"Now, therefore, the *upāṅkyapṛṣṭha* and the *anvāhāryapṛṣṭha* six-day periods. (4)
The ritual procedure for these two is reversed when the Bṛhat and Rathantara are used as the Pṛṣṭha stotras. ||5||
Thus, the meaning is that for all six days, the *rathantara* and *bṛhat* [sāmans] alone should be employed alternately, just as in the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*. ||5||
And of the fourth fortnight. ||6||

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is "of the third and subsequent four-day periods. In the first and second [periods], the ritual action is to be performed according to the original model (prakṛti). ||6||
The *parokṣa* [stotras] are in *bṛhatī* meters for the three days; for the sixth day, they are in *gāyatrī* meters. That is the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) with the *upāṅkya* as the *pṛṣṭha*.

Thus [it is said]. This has been explained. Its arrangement (klṛpti) should be performed like that of the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha of six days. For the latter four-day period, the Mādhyandina-pavamāna should be performed like that of the Upāṃśu-pṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha. The distinction is that on the sixth day, the Vāravantīya is used in place of the Raivata. ||7||

Those same [verses] are used for the Ārbhava [laud] in the subsequent [days]: in the *anuṣṭubh* meters for three days, and in the *gāyatrī* meters for the sixth day. This is the *Anvāhāryapṛṣṭha* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*).

Thus it is clear. The arrangement of the six days should be performed like that of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*. For the subsequent four-day period, the *ārbhavapavamāna* should be performed like that of the *anvāhāryapṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha*. The distinction is that on the sixth day, for the *parisvāna*, the verses are those beginning with *gāyatra-tṛtīya-vaidevanatādyavaidevanata-caturtha-vaidevanatāni*. ||8||
Regarding the nature of the tenth and eleventh days—those characterized by light at the beginning and light at the end—he says:
"Now, therefore, the two six-day periods consisting of light in front and light behind. (6)

Thus: on all six days, he is so described because in the Mādhyandina-pavamāna chants preceding the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, there are "lights" (*jyotīṃṣi*) consisting of the *rathantara*, *bṛhat*, *vairūpa*, *vairāja*, *śākvara*, and *raivata* [sāmans].

The Fourth Chapter: Alternatives for the Pṛṣṭhya-Ṣaḍaha. Regarding the forms of the Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata [Sāmans] in the Ārbhava-stotra following the Pṛṣṭha-lauds: that [sacrifice] is so described because its lights (*jyotis*) consist of these forms. According to the Śruti, "This world is indeed light; this [earth] is indeed the Rathantara," the Rathantara possesses the nature of light due to the non-difference between the earth and the Rathantara. Because they are its offspring, the Vairūpa and Śākvara also possess that nature. Furthermore, "The heavenly world is indeed light."

Because of the Vedic scripture stating "This indeed is the Bṛhat," there is no distinction between the Bṛhat-sāman and heaven; thus, the Bṛhat possesses the nature of light (*jyotis*). Since it is the son of that [Bṛhat], the Vairāja and Raivata also possess it. Because the Rathantara and Bṛhat have the character of day due to their *nidhana* endings being "asa" and "has" respectively, and because day is included within the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*), both possess the nature of light. Furthermore, in the Vairūpa, [it is said] "the quarter, the people, has"; in the Vairāja, "light, has, has raised up"; and since the Śakvarīs are inherently great (*bṛhat*), they possess the nature of the supreme light (*para-jyotis*).

Furthermore, because synonymous terms for "light" (jyotis) exist—such as "the golden ray," "the sun-ray," "the glowing ray," and "the intoxicating ray"—and because the Revatī verses take the form of cows, such that "the cow is indeed light," cows possess the nature of light. Also, in the section concerning the Sarvapṛṣṭha sacrifice, it is stated: "Power is indeed vigor; the Pṛṣṭhas [are power]. "When he offers to Indra associated with the Rathantara, he secures whatever brilliance belongs to Agni; when he offers to Indra associated with the Bṛhat, he secures whatever brilliance belongs to Indra."

According to the Taittirīya Śruti: "Whatever splendor belongs to Indra Vairūpa, that very splendor he acquires; whatever splendor belongs to Indra Vairāja, that very splendor belonging to Dhātṛ he acquires; whatever splendor belongs to Indra Śākvara, that very splendor belonging to the Maruts he acquires; whatever splendor belongs to Indra Raivata, that very splendor belonging to Bṛhaspati he acquires. Furthermore, because the Pṛṣṭhas are taught as non-different from light (*jyotis*), vitality (*ojas*), and splendor (*tejas*), these six Pṛṣṭhas possess the nature of light.

Moreover, the *Rathantara* chant is employed, for the Śruti declares, "The *Rathantara* is indeed Brahman. The *Rathantara* Sāman is used, for the Taittirīya Śruti states, "The *Rathantara* is indeed spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Furthermore, from the Śruti—"Brahman is light; Brahman is the embryo in the wives"—the luminosity of Brahman is established. Having attained the supreme light, one manifests in one's own true form. Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light. Thus it is said: "Om! Water, light, essence, immortality, Brahman."

"That Brahman is water, it is the essence of light. "Having entered into the luminaries by means of the pure [light]," and "That light which shines beyond this heaven—that indeed is this light which is within the person," and so forth; because Brahman has the nature of light according to these passages, the Rathantara possesses the quality of being light (*jyotiṣṭva*). Furthermore, the Śruti demonstrates that the radiance belongs specifically to the letter *bha* in the passage: "Agni shines, the moon shines, the sun shines, the luminaries shine, and the Rathantara shines. Thus, its status as light is established by its very nature.
Because of its vastness and because of its being Brahman, it is therefore designated by the word "Brahman.
The words *bṛhat*, *brahman*, and *mahat* are synonyms expressing the same meaning.

"The Bṛhat-sāman among the Sāmans; born from the waters, born from the cows, born from Truth, born from the mountain, the Truth, the Great; the immeasurable, the Great; I offer salutation to the Great Brahman"—by such Vedic and Smṛti passages, the nature of Brahman belongs to the "Great" (Bṛhat) by its very name. "The mind, indeed, is the Great; like the mind..."

For Prajāpati is the mind; because of the scriptural statement "The mind is Brahman," one should meditate upon the mind as Brahman. One should form a resolve, for according to such Vedic texts as "Consisting of mind, having breath for its body, with the mind as its light, may it enjoy the clarified butter," the mind is the supreme light by nature. Since the Great One (Brahman) possesses that same nature, it too has the nature of light. Furthermore, the fourth chapter contains the alternative arrangements (*anukalpa*) for the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* sacrifice.

"O wielder of the stone, [chant] *mahaḥ* and *mahaḥ*. One should yoke the Self with the mantra *om mahaḥ*, and likewise with the Great Utterance (*mahāvyāhṛti*). Regarding the word *mahaḥ* as a synonym for light, one should meditate on it as "strength" (*ojas*) and "greatness" (*mahaḥ*), because this word *mahaḥ* occurs in its own form within the *pragātha* triplet beginning with *tvām id dhi*. Speech (*vāk*) is indeed the *vairūpa* [sāman]; for it is said, "Speech is both Brahman and Subrahman," and since Prajāpati is speech, the *vairūpa* possesses the nature of Brahman by virtue of being of the nature of speech.

"O wielder of the thunderbolt, a thousand suns [would not equal you]," thus [it is said]. Vaiśampāyana says that it is by this very process, namely the state of having a thousand suns. Regarding this, there is the verse: "O Indra, as many as... may the two worlds follow our birth. Because the Sun, whose nature is Brahman, is established in all the Upaniṣads, and because of the Śruti text, "The Sun is light, light is the Sun," the fact that the Vairūpa [Sāman] is inherently luminous is established precisely by its being the very form of the Sun. [From] Prajāpati [comes] the Vairāja.

Brahman is indeed Prajāpati. "O Brahman, enjoy these [sacrifices] at the shared feast"—because the Vairāja [Sāman] has the nature of Brahman, because it is related to Virāj, and because of the light-nature of the Virāj meter, as well as the statement, "Light indeed was raised up," its status as light is established both by name and by its essential nature through this Śruti. "Sing the Sāman for Indra, the wise one, the great one—the Great [Sāman], the Śakvarī verses, the sacrificial meters, the Truth, the Bṛhat."

"‘To the one made by Brahman, the wise, the praiseworthy’—because the *Bṛhat* [Sāman] is the desire for Indra’s power (*kratu*) and its form is the *Ṛta*, the great, Indra is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *Brahman*. Therefore... they call him who is actually Indra by the name ‘Indra’ as a cryptic designation because of his nature as *Brahman*; and because in the *Pratardana-vidyā* the vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows that same [nature]. If it be argued that this is not so because of the instruction regarding the Self of the speaker, we reply: no, for there is an abundance of references to the inner self (*adhyātma*) in this [text]. Moreover, the instruction is given from the perspective of the sacred scripture (*śāstra*), as in the case of Vāmadeva. If it be argued that it is not so because of the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), [we reply...]

No; for the nature of Brahman has been established by four Brahma-sūtras beginning with "Not so, on account of the threefoldness of meditation" (Upāsātraividhyāt), "On account of being supported," and so forth. Furthermore, because the Mahānāmnīs are named after Indra, Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, Viśvāmitra, Simā, Maḍī, Adhvara, Śakvarī, and others, and because they are associated with Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, Simā, and so on, and since Indra is also Brahman, [Indra is indeed Brahman].
"Light upon light is Indra; Indra is light, the world is light, Indra is light; the sun-rayed one, whose splendor is like a horse's, the ray for exhilaration"—thus [are the verses] of the Mahānāmnīs.

The nature of light (*jyotiṣṭva*) is established both by name and by its essential form. "The *revatī* verses are indeed evil. "The *revatī* verses are the essence of the waters. "O *revatī* waters, you indeed abide as wealth. "The waters, indeed, are called Brahman. "The waters, indeed, are all this. "The waters are the *virāj*. "The waters are indeed immortality"—because the hymn is prepared with such waters, and because the waters named *revatī* are vast, the meters are the waters, the lights are the waters. Light is established in the waters; the waters are established in light.

The luminosity of the waters (ap), the earth (ūrj), and the stars (revatīs) is established by such scriptural passages as, "Hiraṇyajyotis in the midst of the ocean," both by their names and by their essential nature. Likewise, because the six *pṛṣṭha* chants are of the nature of Brahman, because they are highly esteemed as the secret of Brahman, and because they are to be sung in the forest (*araṇyegeya*), their luminosity is well-known. ||9||
He states the alternative arrangement: "The ritual procedure for those two. The indirect *pṛṣṭha* chants [are prescribed] in place of the direct ones;
this is the fourth chapter: the alternative procedures for the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

In the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* of the midday libations, the verses are directly perceived: in *bṛhatīs* for five days, and in *gāyatrīs* for the sixth day; that is the *ṣaḍaha* known as "Light in Front" (*purastāj-jyotis*).

Thus [it is said]. This is clear. The arrangement of this [sacrifice] is as follows: the arrangement for the first and second days should be performed like that of the Upāṅkya and Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍahas. On the first day, at the midday pressing, the Rathantara is in place of the Kaṇvarathantara; the Kaṇvarathantara is the Hotṛ’s *pṛṣṭha* chant. In both these cases, the ritual duties pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* chants must be performed.

In the second [round] at the midday pressing, the Bṛhat [sāman] takes the place of the Kaṇva-Bṛhat; either the Bṛhannidhana Vārka-jambha or the Kaṇva-Bṛhat is the Hotṛ’s Pṛṣṭha. In both cases here, the ritual duties pertaining to the Pṛṣṭha should be performed.

On the midday pressing of the third day, on the *bṛhatī* verses, the *paurumadga* hymn beginning with "abhi soma" is performed on the first verse. The *sāman*-verses of Gautama, Antarikṣa, and Medhātithi are *ubhayataḥstobha*. The *vairūpa* is performed on three verses. The *āṣkāraṇidhana* is on the *madhyā* verse. The *hotṛ-pṛṣṭha* is the short *bṛhat* beginning with "yad dyāvaḥ. Or alternatively: the *paurumadga* beginning with "abhi soma" is on the first verse; the *sāman*-verses of Gautama, Añjoga, Vairūpa, and Medhātithi [follow]; and the *vairūpa* is on three verses.

In the *āṣkāranidhana* [stotra] of the *madhyāsyā*: "yadyāvaḥ" is the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ; or alternatively, "yadyāvaḥ" is the *mahāvaiṣṭambha* *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ. "vayaṃ gha tvā" is the *abhinidhana* *kāṇva* [stotra] of the Brahman. The rest is the same as with the third [day]. However, according to the alternative for the *abhīvarta-kāleya*, "uccā te" is the *gāyatra* on a single verse; the *kṣullakavaiṣṭambha* is on three verses. "abhi soma" constitutes the *sāmatṛcas* of the *paurumadga*, *gautama*, and *antarikṣa*.

On that same *ṛc*-triad are the *sāman*-triads of the *abhīvarta*, *kāleya*, and *aidhātitha*. The *vairūpa* is on three verses. The *āṣkāraṇidhana* is on the *adhyāsya*. "Yadyāvaḥ" is the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha* chant, with the *hrasvā-bṛhat* as its *upaśa*, or alternatively, the *mahāvaiṣṭambha*. "Vayaṃ gha tvā" is the *kāṇva* with the *abhinidhana* for the *brahman*. Or else, "Uccā te" is the *gāyatra* on one verse; the *kṣullakavaiṣṭambha* is on three verses. "Abhi soma" consists of the *paurumadga*, *gautama*, *añjo*, and *vairūpa* chants.

The *sāman*s consist of triplets. The *Sāman*s for the *abhīvarta*, *kāleya*, and *maidhātitha* chants are in triplets. The *vairūpa* is sung over three verses. The *āṣkāra-nidhana* is on the *adhyāsya* verse. "That which [is] heaven" (*yadyāvaḥ*) is the *pṛṣṭha* chant of the Hotṛ; this is the distinction. In both cases here, the ritual duties pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* chants must be performed. The arrangement for the latter three-day period should be carried out according to the model of the *upāṅkya-pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

On the fourth day, at the midday pressing, in place of the *ṛṣabha-vairāja*, there is the *mahāvairāja*. The *ṛṣabha-vairāja* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant of the Hotṛ; or it may be the *sahodairghatamasa*; or the *vasiṣṭhasya vairāja*. In both these cases, the ritual duties pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* chants must be performed.

On the fifth day, during the midday pressing, the *simā* chants take the place of the regular *vatsas*. "In the *trikadrukas*" is the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ; or else, "Come, O Indra" and "O Indra, that which is wonderful" are the first of the *atīṣaṅga* chants. In both cases, the ritual rules pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* must be performed.
In the sixth [day], between the Vājadāvara and the Āryarevata, the specific rule is "dārḍhacyuta. In both these cases, the ritual duties of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] should be performed. ||10||
He states the second [type]:

"Those very same [verses] are used subsequently for the Ārbhava [laud] of the five days; they are used in Anuṣṭubhs for the fifth day and in Gāyatrīs for the sixth. That is the Upariṣṭājyotis six-day period. (11)

The Fourth Chapter: The Alternative Forms of the *Pṛṣṭhya-Ṣaḍaha*. This is clear. Its arrangement is as follows: for the six days, the procedure should be performed like that of the *Sarvaparokṣa-pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*. For the six days, the *Ārbhava-pavamāna* should be performed like that of the *Anvāhārya-pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*. Furthermore, the characteristics of the *pṛṣṭhas* should be applied even to the *Ārbhava-pavamānas* of the six days. On the first day, in place of the *Kaṇvarathantara* in the *Ārbhava*, the *Rathantara* is used; on the second day, in place of the *Kaṇvabṛhat*, the *Bṛhat* is used.

On the third day, at the place of the *hrasvābṛhat* and *upaśa*, there is the *vairūpa* with five *nidhanas*. On the fourth day, at the place of the *ṛṣabha-vairāja*, there is the *mahāvairāja*. On the fifth day, at the place of the *nityavat-sāman*s, there are the *simā*s. Regarding the sixth day, the *Nidāna* states: "In this case, it should be both before and after"; and regarding the *parisvānā*, it says: "If there is a *triṣāman* and an *aiḍa*, the *sāman* should be before the last one. The meaning of this is: in all cases, it is the rule that an adventitious *pṛṣṭha* should be inserted at the end.

The sequence of study is as follows: *prakṛtau parisvāno giriṣṭhā* [is the first], then the Gāyatra, the Tṛtīya, and so on, ending with the Vaidanvatas. Here, since the Brāhmaṇa states "the Vaidanvatas occur" without qualification, when the arrangement is to be made according to the order of the *ajāmi* (non-repetitive) sequence during the deliberations on the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), if the order established by the sequence of study were followed, there would be *jāmi* (repetition/defect) upon the conjunction of the two Vaiḍas—the fourth Vaidanvata and the Raivata. Therefore, he says: "prior to the last."

The sense is that, prior to the last [verse] of the first *vaivanvata* and before the *atitriṣāman*, when the fourth *vaivanvata* has been performed, it is appropriate for the *āgantupṛṣṭha*—whether it be the *aiḍa*, the *raivata*, or the *vāravantīya*—to be inserted at the end. Because the order of study (*adhyayanakrama*) is more authoritative, he states another alternative in accordance with it: "If the *aiḍa* is the last. This means the fourth *vaivanvata*. Prior to the first and fourth *vaivanvatas* among the *sāmans*, the previously mentioned *āgantupṛṣṭha* is to be inserted.

Regarding the *parisvāna* [chanting]: there are the *gāyatratṛtīyavaidavata*, the *raivatādya vaidavata*, and the *caturthavaidavataraivata*. Alternatively, the distinction is that there are the *gāyatratṛtīyavaidavata*, the *caturthavaidavata*, the *ādyavaidavata*, and the *raivatāni*. Thus is the difference. ||11||
[The two *jyotis* sacrifices, with the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* at the beginning and the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* at the end:
He states the nature of the twelve- and thirteen-night periods:

"Now, therefore, there are the two six-day periods, one with the *jyotis* at the beginning preceded by the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*, and the other with the *jyotis* at the end followed by the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*. (12)
Thus; the luminosity of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] is to be explained as before. ||12||
He states the arrangement:

"The ritual procedure for those two is as follows: the *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed in secret; they are reversed when the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are used as the middle-day *pṛṣṭha-stotras* on the *bṛhatī* verses.
That is the six-day rite with the *jyotis* at the beginning, preceded by the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*. (13)

Thus [it is said]. This is clear. The arrangement of the six days should be performed like that of the *ubhayaparokṣapṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha*. For the first and second days, the Mādhyandina-pavamāna should be performed like that of the *purastāj-jyotiḥ-ṣaḍaha*. On the third day, the *paurumadga* [sāman] "abhi soma" is on the first *bṛhatī*; the *rathantara* is on the three [next verses]; the *gautama*, *antarikṣa*, and *aidhātitha* are the *sāmatṛcas*; the *āṣkāraṇidhana* is on the *adhyāsyā*; and the *hrasvā-bṛhat* "yad indra yāvatas tvam" is the *upaśa* for the Hotṛ.

The *pṛṣṭha* [laud]: Alternatively, "O Indra, as great as you are" (*yad indra yāvatas tvam*) is the *mahāvaiṣṭambha* *pṛṣṭha* for the Hotṛ. "We indeed [seek] you" (*vayaṃ gha tvā*) is the *abhinidhana* *kāṇva* for the Brahman. Alternatively, at the midday pressing, in the place of the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*), there is the *añjovairūpa*. "O Indra, as great as you are" (*yad indra yāvatas tvam*) is the intermediate region as the Hotṛ’s *pṛṣṭha*. The rest is the same as with the third [pressing]. However, in the alternative procedure using the *abhīvarta* and *kāleya*, there is the *paurumadga* on the *bṛhatī*: "Toward Soma... (*abhi soma*).

On the first day: the *rathantara* [is the *sāman*] for the *aidhātitha* triplet; the *abhīvarta*, *kāleya*, and *gautama* are the *sāman*-triplets. On the *madhyāsyā* day, there is the *āṣkāraṇidhana*. "O Indra, as much as you are" (*yad indra yāvatas tvam*) is the *hrasva-bṛhat* introductory chant (*upaśa*) for the Hotṛ’s *pṛṣṭha* [laud]. Or alternatively, "O Indra, as much as you are" (*yad indra yāvatas tvam*) is the *mahāvaiṣṭambha* [sāman] for the Hotṛ’s *pṛṣṭha*. "We indeed [thee]" (*vayaṃ gha tvā*) is the fourth chapter—the alternative forms (*anukalpa*) for the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

The *abhinidhana* is the *kāṇva* of the Brahman priest; or alternatively, "abhi soma" is the *paurumadga* in the first [verse]. The *rathantara*, *aidhātitha*, *jīva*, and *vairūpa* are the *sāmatṛcas*. The *abhīvarta*, *kāleya*, and *gautama* are the *sāmatṛcas*. The *āṣkāraṇidhana* is in the *adhyāsyā*. "yad indra yāvatas tvam" is the *antarikṣa* *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ. Such is the distinction.
On the fourth day, the midday *pavamāna* should be performed like that of the *jyotiḥ-ṣaḍaha*. The distinction is that at midday, the *bṛhat* [sāman] takes the place of the *vairāja*.

On the fifth day, the *soma* chant "soma u ṣvā" is performed on the *bṛhatī* meter; the *ākūpāra* and *rathantara* are the two triplets; the *hārāyaṇa*, *mānava*, and *vāma* are the triplets of *sāmans*; and the *triṇidhana* of Agni is performed on three verses—this is the distinction. However, when the *abhīvarta* and *kāleya* are used, the *soma u ṣvā* is on the *bṛhatī* meter; the *ānūpa* is on the first verse; the *rathantara* is on three verses; the *hārāyaṇa* and *mānava* are on the first verse; the *vāma*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya* are the triplets of *sāmans*; and the *triṇidhana* of Agni is on three verses—this is the distinction.

In the sixth [day], regarding the *bṛhatī* [verse] beginning with "mṛjyamānaḥ," there are the *svāra-aukṣṇorandhra*, the *aiḍamaukṣṇorandhra*, and the *vājijit* as *sāmatṛcas*. The *varuṇasāman*, *goṣṭha*, *kaulmalabarhiṣa*, and *bṛhat* are on triplets (*tṛcas*). However, in the alternative (*anukalpa*) for the *abhīvarta* and *kāleya*, the *nidāna* states here: "But in the sixth, if it is the *bṛhat*, it is a *sāmatṛca*. Thus, "mṛjyamānaḥ" consists of the *aiḍamaukṣṇorandhra*, *abhīvarta*, and *kāleya* as *sāmatṛcas*; the *svāra-aukṣṇorandhra* is on three verses; the *vājajit*, *kaulmalabarhiṣa*, and *bṛhat* are *sāmatṛcas*;
and the *varuṇasāman* and *goṣṭha* are on two triplets. This is the distinction. ||13||
He states the second form: "Those same [verses] are reversed in the *ārbhava* *anuṣṭubh*s later on; that is the *bṛhat-rathantara-upariṣṭāj-jyotis* six-day period. (14)

Thus [it is said]. This is clear. Its arrangement (*klṛpti*) is as follows: the arrangement should be made like that of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) with both types of *pṛṣṭha* chants performed indirectly (*parokṣa*). Above the first five days, there is the *jyotis*.

The Ārbhava-pavamāna chant should be performed like that of the *ṣaḍaha* (six-day rite). On the third day, at the Ārbhava-stotra, the *Gaurīvita* and *Tatriṇidhana* *Tvāṣṭrī-sāmans* are placed on the first *ṛc*. The *Svāra-tvāṣṭrī-sāman* and the *Rathantara* are on the two subsequent *ṛcs*. On the fourth day, the *Bṛhat* is in the place of the *Vairāja*. On the fifth day, there are the *Gaurīvita*, *Ṛṣabha*, *Śākvara*, *Pārtha*, *Aṣṭeḍa-padastobha*, *Rathantara*, and *Ātreya* [sāmans]. Here, as with the *Śakvarī*, if the final [verse] of the inserted *pṛṣṭha-stotra* were to coincide with the *Dāśaspatya*, it would result in a ritual redundancy (*jāmi*).

To prevent that [undesired consequence], the assumption of "being penultimate" is made. However, in the case of the *samūḍha* [chanting], there is this distinction: "Pavasva vājasātaye," the *gaurīvita*, the *padanidhana*, the *śuddha-āśuddhīya*, the *ṛṣabha*, the *śākvara*, the *ākūpāra*, the *aṣṭeḍa*, the *padastobha*, and the *rathantara*.

Regarding the sixth day: the underlying principle (*nidāna*) here is that on the sixth day, the *bṛhatī* verses from the *gaurīvita* are arranged in reverse order. The rule (*sūtra*) regarding this is: "From the *madhuścunnidhana* up to the *ākūpāra*. And since it is said, "On the sixth day, the *bṛhatī* is arranged," the meaning is that there are three single-verse hymns (*ekarcas*) following the *bṛhatī*. In the *ārbhava* [śastra], for the *anuṣṭubh* verses, the *gaurīvita-bṛhatī* consists of two triplets (*tṛcas*). The *sāman*-triplets are the *ākūpāra*, *madhuścunnidhana*, and *vāṅnidhana-krauñca*; or alternatively, the *vāṅnidhana-krauñca*, *madhuścunnidhana*, and *ākūpāra*. The *aiḍa* and *krauñca* [sāmans] are sung over three verses. Such is the distinction.

Regarding the *samūḍha* [chanting], the rule here is: "In the *samūḍha*, [the final syllable] is the penultimate. For the two triplets beginning with "The Soma juices flow" (*somāḥ pavante*), there are the *gaurīvita* and *madhuścunnidhana* [melodies].
The *vāṅnidhana*, *krauñcaiḍa*, *krauñcākūpāra*, and [other] *sāman*-triplets [are used]. The specific distinction is that the *bṛhat* [is applied] to three verses. ||14||
Thus ends the twelfth section of the second chapter.
The Fourth Chapter: Alternative Forms of the Pṛṣṭhya-Ṣaḍaha;
Thirteenth Section: [The Pṛṣṭhas with the Parokṣāpṛkṣya and the Pratyakṣāpṛkṣya]

He states the nature of the fourteenth and fifteenth [days]: "Now, therefore, follows the six-day period characterized by the *āparkya* and *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. The word *āparkya* is derived from the root *pṛc* preceded by the prefix *ā*, with the Vedic suffix *ṇyat* added to form *saṃparka*; here, the prefix *ā* is used in the sense of "slightly" (*īṣad*). Thus, *āparkya* means "slightly connected. Because the *pṛṣṭha* stotras have a slight connection with both the indirect (*parokṣa*) and direct (*pratyakṣa*) forms in the middle cycle (*madhyamaparyāya*), they possess the quality of being *āparkya*. Those two [six-day periods] are thus described as having *āparkya-pṛṣṭha* stotras. He provides the designation for both based on their difference in ritual characteristics:
The *parokṣāparkya* with the *pṛṣṭha* chant and the *pratyakṣāparkya* with the *pṛṣṭha* chant. ||1||
Thus [ends the first section]. ||1||
He states the arrangement:

"The ritual procedure for those two is as follows. For the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there are the first and last turns (*paryāya*); for the indirect perception (*parokṣa*), there is the middle one. That is the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) consisting of the *parokṣa-pṛṣṭha*. (2)

Thus it is clear. For the first day, the first and last *paryāyas* belong to the *rathantara*; in that same triplet (*tṛca*), the middle one belongs to the *kaṇvarathantara*. This constitutes the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ. Everything else is the same as on the first day.

For the second day: the first and last rounds (*paryāya*) are from the *Bṛhat* [Sāman], beginning with "tvām id dhi havāmahe. In that same triplet (*ṛca*), the middle [round] is from the *Bṛhannidhana*, the *Vārkañjabha*, or the *Kaṇvabṛhat*. This is the *Pṛṣṭha* Stotra of the Hotṛ. Everything else is the same as on the second day.

For the third day: the first and last *paryāyas* of the *vairūpa* [stotra] consist of the triplet beginning with "yad dyāvaḥ. In that same triplet, there are the *hrasva*, *bṛhat*, and *upaśa* chants; this is the middle *paryāya* of either the *antarikṣa* or the *mahāvaiṣṭambha*. Thus is the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ in the case of the *antarikṣa* [pakṣa]. At the midday pressing, in the place of the *antarikṣa*, there is the *añjovairūpa* in the case of the *mahāvaiṣṭambha* [pakṣa]. The *kāṇva* chant for the Brahman priest has the *abhinidhana* ending, "vayaṃ gha tvā. The rest is the same as on the third day.

For the fourth day: the first and last *paryāyas* are [the hymns] of Mahāvairāja, beginning with "Drink the Soma" (*pibā soma*). In that same triplet (*tṛca*), the middle [verse] belongs either to Ṛṣabha Vairāja, or to Sahoda Dairghatamasa, or to Vasiṣṭha Vairāja. This is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* of the Hotṛ. The rest is the same as on the fourth day.

[The ritual] of the fifth day. Herein is the underlying principle (*nidāna*): "But on the fifth [day], because of the division, there is no other [chanting] among the *Mahānāmnī* verses. In these verses beginning with *vidā maghavan*, the first and last rounds (*paryāya*) belong to the *Mahānāmnīs*. The middle [round] belongs to the *Nityavatsās* (the "Always-Calf" verses), or alternatively, to the first of the *Atīṣaṅgas*. In these *Gāyatrī* and *Anuṣṭubh* verses beginning with *indrāyāhi* and *yadindra citram*, [these are the chants]. Thus is the *Pṛṣṭha-stotra* of the Hotṛ. The rest is the same as on the fifth day.

Regarding the sixth day: here the underlying principle (nidāna) is that because there are two [verses] in the *prāṅkya* and other [stomas], the *vāravantīya* should be chanted according to the meter (*chandas*). The alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) for both *pavamāna* chants follows the sequence of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, or it is due to the diversity of the *stotrīya* verses. Furthermore, there is the attainment of the manifest (*pratyakṣa*) and the unmanifest (*parokṣa*), and because of the common instruction (*samānādeśa*). Both [chants] belong to the *pāvamāna*; by connection with the *revatī* verses, the *vāravantīya* serves the manifest purpose, and by the *dārḍhacyuta*, it serves the unmanifest purpose.

"They are manifest" (*pratyakṣāṇi*) because they follow the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] by nature; "they are unmanifest" (*parokṣāṇi*) because of being unmanifest on both sides, due to the completeness of the manifestation, and because of the observation of the *garbha*. Or rather, they are manifest in a single *tṛca*, because the *viṣṭutis* have the *tṛca* as their scope and because both types are observed there. But it is not so in the fifth [day], because of the difference. "There is no other [rule] regarding the *Mahānāmnīs*.
Here ends the fourth chapter: The alternatives for the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

The section beginning with "In the *prāṅkya* and others" and ending with "in the sequence of the *pṛṣṭhas*" constitutes a single sūtra. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the *pratyakṣa*, *parokṣa*, *prāṅkya-pratyakṣa*, and *parokṣāparkya* [six-day rites]. Regarding the phrase "because of having two-fold nature" (*dviṣāmatvāt*): in the six-day rites such as the *prāṅkya*, because the author of the ritual manual (*kalpakāra*) has placed the *sāmans* that are both manifest (*pratyakṣa*) and hidden (*parokṣa*) for each day among the *pṛṣṭhas*, they possess a two-fold nature.

Since it was previously stated by [the author] himself that the sixth day has two *pṛṣṭha* [stotras], and because here both the *pavamāna* and the *pṛṣṭha* must be praised with two *sāmans* each, [the author] says "or the *Chandasya*" regarding the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ, even though two *sāmans* would otherwise be obtained; the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "only" (*eva*). Thus, the meaning is that there is only one *sāman*, the Vāravantīya, upon the triplet beginning with "revatīr naḥ. This triplet itself possesses the nature of being both manifest and unmanifest. Therefore, the meaning is that the Vāravantīya alone is the *sāman*.

And it was stated by him himself in the *Pūrvanidānasūtra*: "Now, on the sixth day, when the *Revatī* verses are used, the *Vāravantīya* becomes the *pṛṣṭha* stotra. Regarding this, some state it directly (*pratyakṣam*), while others state that the indirectness (*pārokṣya*) of the *Vāravantīya* is precisely the indirectness of the *Revatī* verses. Furthermore, in the *Uttaranidānasūtra*, he will state later on: "Now, where [the verses] are indirect, there the *Vāravantīya* [is applied]."

By this, they consider that both of these are indeed perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). Of those two, however, one follows the rule (*anudharma*) of the other *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. In this regard, it is not the case that for the two *parokṣa-pṛṣṭhas*, the *revatīs* follow the rule. Furthermore, by the author of the *Kalpa*, since the original (*prākṛta*) six-day period is perceptible, and because the *vāravantīya* has been conceived as having both perceptible and imperceptible forms within the entirely *parokṣa*, the dual-natured (*ubhayaparokṣa*) six-day period, and the *anugṛhītaparokṣa* [period], its dual nature is established.

Therefore, just as in the case of the five-day sacrifice (*pañcāha*), on the sixth day, for the sake of the two *sāmans*—one perceptible and one imperceptible—one should perform the *vāravantīya* as a single *sāman* upon the triplet beginning with "revatīr na" (Revatīr naḥ). This is the intended meaning. Lest there be a misconception that, as in the case of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, one might imagine a similar dual nature for the single Raivata *sāman* during the *pavamāna* stotra, he says: "The alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) for both [applies] to the *pavamāna*. This means it applies to both the Raivata and the Dārḍhacyuta. The arrangement according to the sequence of the *pṛṣṭhas* is the determination made by the authors of the ritual manuals (*kalpakāra*).

The meaning is that the sequence of these two [stotras] should be determined in accordance with the distinction between the perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and the non-perceptible (*parokṣa*). He states another alternative: "Or because of the plurality of *stotrīya* verses. Because of the difference in the *tṛca* (three-verse hymn) in the case of "revatīr no revatīnām indra," there is no perceptibility in the preceding *tṛca*, nor is there non-perceptibility in the subsequent *tṛca*. Regarding the attainment of a plurality of *stotrīya* verses in the *pavamāna* chant as in the *pṛṣṭha* chant, he says: "And because of the common instruction, both belong to the *pavamāna*," meaning that both *sāmans* should be performed within a single *tṛca*.

Since it is prescribed by the author of the Kalpa-sūtra that both the *Raivata* and the *Dārḍhacyuta*, which are of the nature of direct and indirect [forms], belong to the *Pavamāna* hymns within a single identical *tṛca*, even under the view that there is a plurality of *stotrīya* verses in the *pṛṣṭha* stotra, the *Vāravantīya* should remain only one, serving the purpose of the direct and indirect forms as before; therefore, he says: "Because of the connection with the *Revatī* verses. He states the justification for this position: "The direct ones... [and] "...from the original *pṛṣṭhya*."

The sense is that the plural designation "pratyakṣāṇi" (directly perceived) is used because, even in this six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), the *pārṣṭhika* *sāmans* belonging to the ordinary [days] are also conceived as being *pṛṣṭhya*. "On account of being indirect on both sides" means on account of being separated from both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*. "On account of the completeness of what is directly perceived" means because the *Vāravantīya* is prescribed as being directly perceived everywhere in terms of both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*. And "because of the observation of the pregnant [verse]."

Because two *sāmans* are seen in two *ṛc*-triplets at the *pṛṣṭha* of the *aptoryāma*, and because they are likewise seen in such passages as "eight pregnant [cows]," etc.; and because in the preceding days, such as the *prāyaṇīya*, only a single *ṛc*-triplet contains both a direct and an indirect *sāman*; therefore, the assumption of two *sāmans* in two *ṛc*-triplets on this sixth day is improper. Due to this lack of consensus, he states another alternative: "or in a single *ṛc*-triplet. That is, the *vāravantīya* and *dārḍhacyuta* *sāmans* should be applied to the single *ṛc*-triplet beginning with "revatīr naḥ."

He states the reason for this: "In the case of those [hymns] that are directly perceived (*pratyakṣeṣu*). This refers to the *tṛcas* (three-verse hymns) such as "abhi tvā śūra" and others; because the *viṣṭutis* (modes of chanting) belong to the *stotras* (hymns of praise), and since the context concerns the *tṛcas*, it follows that they apply to each individual *tṛca*. Thus, both [the *viṣṭutis* and the *stotras*] are established within the single *tṛca*.
[End of] Chapter Four: The Alternative Forms of the *Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.

The sense is that since the *rathantara*, *kaṇvarathantara*, and so forth are seen only in a single *ṛc* triplet, here too the *vāravantīya* and *dārḍhacyuta* must be assumed to apply to the triplet beginning with "revatīr naḥ. Thus, regarding the fifth day as well, when two *sāmans* would apply to a single triplet, he says: "But not on the fifth," because of its difference. "Because of its difference" means because of its difference from the preceding days. He explains that very point: "Not another [is applied] to the *mahānāmnīs*."

The meaning is that since no other *sāman* is observed in the scriptural recitation (*śruti*) for the *mahānāmnī* verses beginning with "vidā maghavan," two *sāmans* are fixed for each pair of triplets (*tṛca*). Its arrangement (*klṛpti*) is as follows: for the first triplet, the *gāyatra*, *aiṣovṛdhīya*, *krauñca*, *vājadāvarya*, *raivata*, and *dārḍhacyuta*; for the second triplet, the *svāra*, *aukṣṇorandhra*, *aiḍamaukṣṇorandhra*, and *aukṣṇorandhra*; or alternatively, the *aiḍamaukṣṇorandhra*, *svāra*, and *aukṣṇorandhra*. For the third triplet, the *kaulmalabarhiṣa*, *vājajit*, and *varuṇasāman* are the *sāmans*. These constitute the *sāmatṛcas*.

The *goṣṭha* [stotra] is performed in three [verses]. The *vāmadevya*, beginning with "etam u tyam," is at the end, as in the *ihavat* [rite]. The *vāravantīya* is the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ, beginning with "revatīr naḥ. Alternatively, the first and last rounds (*paryāya*) of the *vāravantīya* consist of the verses beginning with "revatīr naḥ"; the middle round belongs to the *dārḍhacyuta*, beginning with "revām indre vaḥ. Or else, the first and last rounds of the *vāravantīya* consist of the verses beginning with "revatīr naḥ," while the middle round of the *dārḍhacyuta* is on that same triplet (*tṛca*). The rest is the same as in the sixth [day].
He states the second [point]:

the first and last turnings belong to that which is out of sight; the middle one belongs to that which is directly perceived. That is the six-day rite (ṣaḍaha) following upon the direct perception and the comparison. 3.

Thus [it is stated]. This is clear. Regarding the first day: the first and last *paryāyas* of the *kaṇvarathantara* are [performed] with the hymn "Abhi tvā śūra" (RV 7.32). In that same triplet (*tṛca*), the middle [verse] is for the *rathantara*. Thus is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* of the Hotṛ. Everything else is the same as on the first day.

For the second day: "tvāmiddhi" is the *kaṇvabṛhat* or the *bṛhannidhana* of *arkajambha*; its first and last *paryāyas* are the same. In that same triplet, the middle [verse] is the *bṛhat*, which constitutes the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* of the Hotṛ. The rest is the same as on the second day.

Regarding the third day: for the first and last rounds, the *hrasvā-bṛhat* is used as the *upaśa*; [this belongs] to the *antarikṣa* or the *mahāvaiṣṭambha*. On that same triplet (*ṛca*), the middle [round] belongs to the *vairūpa*. This is the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ. In the case of the *antarikṣa*, at the midday pressing, the *añjovairūpa* takes the place of the *antarikṣa*. In the case of the *mahāvaiṣṭambha*, "vayaṃ gha tvā" with the *abhinidhana* is the *kāṇva* [sāman] for the Brahman priest. This is the distinction; everything else is the same as on the third day.

For the fourth day: the first and last *paryāyas* consist of the verses beginning with "Drink the Soma," belonging either to Ṛṣabha Vairāja, or to Sahoda Dīrghatamas, or to Vasiṣṭha Vairāja. On that same triplet, the middle verse belongs to Mahāvairāja; this constitutes the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* of the Hotṛ. Everything else is the same as on the fourth [day].
